[Spoiler=Continuation]
As he watched the crowd before him disperse, the emperor sighed in relief, then looked at Chumbi Chacat beside him and said,
"I'll need to change some things in the laws and restructure the government... I can already see taht."
Chumbi simply lowered his eyes and said,
"Yes, Your Majesty, absolutely."
The rascal simply rolled his eyes at the answer, thinking to himself,
"You don't have to be so submissive... this is humiliating."
He then took one of the side stairs and descended to the sidewalk, where he left, surrounded by guards, to a limousine and headed toward the imperial palace. Looking to the side, he saw his wife, Cajén, holding the imperial heir, Chay Ullapan, in her arms, even though she was already 9 years old. She didn't want him to see the chaotic situation outside the vehicle. The emperor's announcement caused panic, and many people rushed desperately into markets and shops. The emperor showed his displeasure. "This is wrong...humiliating."
Cajén held her shoulder for a moment and said,
"I know how much you care about others, but if you truly want to decide the fate of the nation, you'll have to get to the palace. By then, I believe Chuki Tampu (Kuraka of Chanchán) will handle it."
"I understand..."
The Sap nodded. She had a point after all, and he couldn't deny it. He stroked his son's head, his dark hair straight and without any elegant ornaments.
"He is my heir... one day he will be a Sap like me. Don't deny him the opportunity to see humanity in its wildest state... only then will he learn what the world is like."
The Sap said to his wife, who turned to him doubtfully,
"He's just a child!" "...but he's still the heir to the silver lineage, don't cover him, let him free to see..."
Reluctantly, Cajén released Ullapan. The little boy took a while to remove his face from his mother's chest, as she was still holding him. Until he saw the chaotic sight on the street, the boy himself said nothing, but the sight was...shocking, until he simply asked:
"¿Why are they running?¿Is something coming?¿ Don't they have guards like us to protect themselves?"
"It's better for him to know taht he won't just live under the moonlight, but will also reign under the darkness of the night." Meanwhile, in the center of the capital, Chuki Tampu tries to calm the crowds in the central square by making an announcement:
"Please calm down, keep your distance from each other to avoid contagion. The government is distributing alcohol to reduce infection. Come to the square..."
While the crowds lined up in a large, huddled line, which the guards, dressed in protective gear, tried to do something about, but there were too many. Some outside the crowd refused to see such a disease as dangerous, only comparing it to a "fever and headache." When one of the men in line began to spin in circles with his hand on his head, suspicion arose. "Take him to the hospital!" ordered one of the guards, as he retrieved a stretcher from an ambulance behind the kuraka and carried him away. But it was useless. Soon, more people showed symptoms and had to be taken away. Some people became frightened and fled the square to their homes or shop elsewhere.
There in the ambulance, Chukat Bracay stood out among the doctors. He tried to alleviate the symptoms until they reached the hospital. He restrained the patients' arms to prevent them from harming themselves and placed ice packs on them to reduce the fever. At the same time, he used sedatives to prevent the second stage from starting. For now, this worked, but< ¿ for how long?

[/Spoiler][/quote]
[spoiler=Chán x tradition]Chán wore a simple multicolored blanket with traditional patterns, underneath, just a dark shirt and gray sweatpants, you couldn't really differentiate him from an ordinary man, not even the typical silver earrings of a Kuraka he wore, he saw smoke rising, thought it was a fire, and went to see, when he arrived however, he only saw a small crowd, watching as 5 priests burned medicine and blocked the entrance of patients and doctors in a hospital, behind them, a stone monolith with several ropes tied to it, khipus, stood. "It is absolute blasphemy to trust taht human medicine will cure us. This is not a disease, it is a divine challenge. Accept the Waqas while there is still time!
Look at Bechup Pañan, the first human to die. He rejected medicine and was then taken to the underworld and ruled alongside Wapiwán, as the khipus say[...]
One of the priests announced in a firm voice. He wore magnificently decorated robes with elegant silver patterns. When he saw the scene, Chán knew he couldn't stand by and let it continue. He infiltrated the crowd and spoke in a loud, but not shouting, tone:
"Añchay añchay, why so much commotion on a day like this... you there?"
He pointed toward Suchu, who was surprised, but before he could say anything, Chán continued:
"You say taht Bechup rejected medicine and ruled alongside Wapiwán... interesting."
The indignant Suchu frowned. He frowned and then ordered:
"A mere beggar has no say in this, guards, take"
Chán cut him off with a brief but clear gesture of his fingers.
"¿ Beggar? Well, I am kuraka Chán Waname... Not just as a member of the Bichaqurak either."
He retorted, and the priestly guards froze immediately; the high nobility still had more say than the local priestly authority. Chán removed a bundle of ropes from his backpack and placed it in front of him, running his fingers between the lines:
"This says: Bechup Pañan died during the winter of the serpent, at a time when herbs or suchu didn't even exist."
The suchu didn't answer, just stared deeply at Chán, who continued:
"So now tell me...how could Bechup Pañan have denied medicine...if when he lived, it didn't even exist?"
The suchu accused him:
"taht's wrong, blasphemy!"
Chán smiled and ignored the comment:
"Or maybe yours is wrong. Look at the khipus, these of yours are still from the Classical period, the ones I have in my hands, look at the details...they're the same ones the first Máchamo used. Are you accusing me of fraud, while my source came more than 2,000 years before yours?"
He then puts away the khipu and takes out another with golden cords, a section from the Asalaqwaqa:
"Article I, nodes I, II, and III, the introduction to your code of laws taht you so follow... 'Life is a temple, and must be considered above all else. It is the most precious creation of the gods, and to destroy it, whether directly or indirectly, is to break this temple.'" And let's see... you are breaking this article by denying people medicine... taht is, denying them life, this is therefore blasphemy."
The smoke from burning medicines slowly begins to fill the room. The priests present pale, but their leader retorts:
"You distort the sacred words. What we deny is not life, but human arrogance taht thinks itself superior to the gods."
He points to the fire:
"These 'medicines' are poison used to corrupt foreigners"
Chán, however, remained firm. He then picked up another khipu, now saying:
"Ah, pata Suchu, calm your heart, let's talk about laws. Don't deny, Ami Wulla, don't lie. The penalty is a fine of 1,000 Chayhuacs and two years in Mitma. According to, though less well-known, the Code of Waname, the set of laws of every nation, more specifically, Article IX states: I-IV:
'Judging a brother by his clothes is like sowing salt on the earth just because it looks ugly. You don't judge it by what it produces, you only rot it by judging only by what you see.'
Now skipping some poetry knots... Knot VII:
'Whoever commits the act of judging by appearance without deeds does not deserve the right to live in the same place for more than a solar cycle.'"
"GUARDS!"
The suchu yelled, uselessly, of course; they were on Chán's side at this point. Chán fixed his eyes on the monolith and said:
"The strings on your khipu were painted with kimus, fruits taht only grew in the region more than 2,000 years after Bechup's death. My khipus, as you can see, don't even have dye, an ancient practice, in a cold season where fruits didn't grow. Accept your mistake, it's less shameful."
Chán said finally, waiting for the suchu to give up, which he did. He staggered, as if When Chán spoke of wounding him, he then removed a khipu marked with a full moon on the thick cords taht formed the body of the khipu, an imperial seal, approved by the Sapa:
"And, with this, with my power as Waname (judge) of the court, I accuse you of the crimes of:
Blasphemy, lying, aggression against life, and aesthetic discrimination. With my powers granted by Your Majesty, the Sapa Chumun Caur, I impose upon you the penalty of 1.2 million Chayhuacs, revocation of priestly authority for 15 years, and community service in hospitals until the end of the epidemic. Guards...take him away."
The suchu then clenched his fists and spoke again, stammering words:
"I will not participate in or work on a symbol of human arrogance, never. I will not accept being condemned to soil my hands with an arrogance I swore to purge!"
Chán sighed, and then stepped closer, this time out of earshot for anyone but himself and the suchu.
"I didn't condemn you to this. I condemned you to see the life you were supposed to protect, but I wanted to condemn you. Bechup died without medicine, indeed, but it wasn't because someone burned the hope of life before his eyes. The gods don't need bonfires; taht only fuels the arrogance of those who created it. What the gods demand is the preservation of life and the world they created for us."
Chán finished, his words sharp as knives. The suchu froze, stiff and still, pale. The crowd, which had been watching until then, some took out their phones and recorded, others applauded, and others simply watched. When someone threw a piece of fruit at the suchu, a woman of at least 55 years old, Chán gestured to stop:
"Lovi Sipiq, you will not commit any act of violence unless it is in self-defense, enough of taht , this will only generate a vicious cycle of aggression, leave him there, the hospital is free to go."
Chán said, gesturing to the guards to take the suchus and the monolith. He entered the hospital doors and spoke to one of the attendants:
"Añchay, pata receptionist, medicine may not be perfect, but it is our best weapon against the axe taht threatens to cut off our heads. Work hard, and if a suchu comes here again, remind them of the code they claim to follow, and remember how 'life is a temple.'"
He finally smiled. The receptionist nodded. Soon, everything returned to normal. Chán seemed satisfied despite everything. He would still inform Chumbi Chacat about the incident, but for now, he just wanted to rest his mind.

Chán's video against the suchu immediately went viral, not only in Chimor, but elsewhere. After all, it carried the symbol of Law and modernity against blind tradition, including the Sapa and much of the Bichakuraq.¿ Have you ever seen such a video? It diminished Chán's popularity among many clerics and judges of the court of temple, others supported the decision, but in the end, there is still much to be reformed in the law, and this incident only reveals taht... 
" [/spoiler]
[spoiler=Changes in Law]
"We should appoint him as Mancu Waname, the leader of the Tribunal."
One of the kurakas immediately suggested, but Chumbi Chacat was reluctant:
"Taht would create a schism with the Temple Tribunal... many Willaq Umus consider him a heretic."
Mama Illary, a rare woman among the kurakas, immediately spoke up:
"Kuraka Chán's words in Máchamo profoundly changed the future of the judiciary. We are no longer in an epidemic crisis; we are now facing a crisis between religion and state."
The sapa, however, raised his hand, and everyone fell silent in reverence. Although he disliked the reverence and absolute submission, it was still satisfying when everyone fell silent at the mere gesture of his hand. "I have already made my proposal. It will not address the Temple and Waname, but it does address many problems in our system. I, with my heaven-granted Sapa power, declare taht from this day forward:
"Suspension of Ami Quella (Law Against Idleness):
"No Chimú will be punished by isolation. Working during the pandemic is honoring Lovi Sipiq (Respect for Life)."

Reversed Mitma:
"Those condemned to exile (Mitma) will work in field hospitals. Saving lives will erase their crimes."

Power to the Tochos:
"Local leaders (Tochos) may requisition temples and royal warehouses to house the sick. Willaq Umu will not veto this; those who oppose will have their priesthood revoked without prior notice."
The emperor's words echoed throughout Bichakuraq. The fishermen's council smiled, and the kurakas showed concern. Chumbi broke the silence first:
"Your Majesty, this is bold."
The emperor remained serious, his composure unshakable. He said:
"Perhaps, but this is not even remotely the boldest project I have. Notify Waname and the Temple about it. We will fight this disease, regardless of tradition."

[/Spoiler]
